'''Thomas E. Cravens''' is an American space physicist and Professor Emeritus<ref name="KU Physics Bio Emeritus">{{cite web |url=https://physics.ku.edu/people/emeritus-faculty |title=Emeritus Faculty |publisher=University of Kansas, Department of Physics and Astronomy |access-date=2025-04-10 |quote=Thomas Cravens, Professor Emeritus}}</ref> in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Kansas]].<ref name="KU Physics Bio">{{cite web |url=https://physics.ku.edu/people/cravens-thomas |title=Thomas Cravens |publisher=University of Kansas, Department of Physics and Astronomy |access-date=2025-04-10}}</ref> He is known for developing the widely accepted model explaining the emission of [[X-rays]] from [[comets]], a phenomenon discovered unexpectedly in 1996.<ref name="Cravens 1997">{{cite journal |last1=Cravens |first1=T. E. |title=Comet Hyakutake x-ray source: Charge transfer of solar wind heavy ions |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=105–108 |year=1997 |doi=10.1029/96GL03780 |bibcode=1997GeoRL..24..105C }}</ref><ref name="RosatXray">{{cite web |url= https://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/rosat/hyakutake/rosat3_24.html| title= X-Rays From Comet Hyakutake Discovered by ROSAT |publisher= NASA HEASARC |date=May 7, 1996 |access-date=2025-04-10}}</ref><ref name="DennerlReview">{{cite journal |last1=Dennerl |first1=K. |title=X-rays from comets |journal=Space Science Reviews |volume=157 |issue=1–4 |pages=57–91 |year=2010 |doi=10.1007/s11214-010-9720-5 |bibcode=2010SSRv..157...57D |quote=The most likely process responsible for cometary X-ray emission is charge exchange (CX) between highly charged heavy ions of the solar wind and cometary neutrals (Cravens 1997).|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Cravens received his B.A. in physics from [[Stony Brook University|State University of New York at Stony Brook]] in 1970.<ref name="KU Physics Bio" /> He then pursued graduate studies at [[Harvard University]], where he earned his Ph.D. in astronomy in 1975 under the supervision of [[Alex Dalgarno]].<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/><ref name="HarvardThesis"/> His doctoral dissertation was titled "Astrophysical Applications of Electron Energy Deposition in Molecular Hydrogen.".<ref name="HarvardThesis"/>

== Career ==

After receiving his Ph.D., Cravens worked at the Space Physics Research Laboratory at the [[University of Michigan]].<ref name="MichiganSPR"/> He later joined the faculty of the [[University of Kansas]] Department of Physics and Astronomy, where he is currently a Professor Emeritus.<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/><ref name="KU Physics Bio Emeritus"/>

His research spans a range of topics in [[space plasma physics]], focusing on the interactions of the [[solar wind]] with planets (including Earth, Mars, Venus, and the outer planets) and comets.<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/> He also investigates the physics of planetary ionospheres and magnetospheres, and the [[interstellar medium]].<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/>

== Cometary X-ray emission ==

A significant contribution by Cravens is his model explaining the emission of [[X-rays]] from comets.<ref name="Cravens 1997" /><ref name="Bhardwaj 2007">{{cite journal |last1=Bhardwaj |first1=A. |last2=Elsner |first2=R. F. |last3=Gladstone |first3=G. R. |last4=Cravens |first4=T. E. |last5=Lisse |first5=C. M. |last6=Waite Jr |first6=J. H. |title=X-rays from solar system objects |journal=Planetary and Space Science |volume=55 |issue=9 |pages=1135–1189 |year=2007 |doi=10.1016/j.pss.2006.11.011 |arxiv=1012.1088 |bibcode=2007P&SS...55.1135B}}</ref><ref name="DennerlReview"/> Prior to the observation of X-rays from [[Comet Hyakutake]] in 1996 by the [[ROSAT]] satellite, cold bodies like comets were not generally expected to be significant X-ray sources.<ref name="RosatXray"/>

Cravens proposed that the primary mechanism is charge exchange (also known as charge transfer) between highly charged heavy ions in the solar wind and neutral atoms and molecules in the cometary coma.<ref name="Cravens 1997" /> The solar wind contains ions such as O<sup>6+</sup>, O<sup>7+</sup>, C<sup>5+</sup>, and C<sup>6+</sup>. When these ions encounter the neutral gas sublimating from the comet's nucleus (the coma), they can capture electrons from the neutral species (e.g., H<sub>2</sub>O, CO<sub>2</sub>, CO).<ref name="Cravens 1997" /><ref name="DennerlReview"/>

The process can be represented as:

:X<sup>q+</sup> + M → X<sup>(q-1)+</sup>\* + M<sup>+</sup>

where X<sup>q+</sup> is a highly charged solar wind ion, M is a neutral cometary molecule, X<sup>(q-1)+</sup>\* is the resulting ion in an excited state after capturing an electron, and M<sup>+</sup> is the newly ionized cometary molecule.

The excited ion (X<sup>(q-1)+</sup>\*) rapidly relaxes to a lower energy state by emitting a photon, typically in the X-ray or extreme ultraviolet (EUV) part of the spectrum. The photon's energy reflects the large energy difference between the ion's states.<ref name="Cravens 1997" /><ref name="DennerlReview"/>

Cravens' model successfully explained the observed spectral characteristics and spatial distribution of cometary X-rays.<ref name="Cravens 1997" /><ref name="DennerlReview"/> This discovery provided a new tool for studying both cometary atmospheres and the composition (particularly the heavy ion component) of the solar wind.<ref name="DennerlReview"/> The charge exchange mechanism identified by Cravens is now recognized as an important X-ray emission process in various astrophysical environments, such as planetary atmospheres and the heliosphere.<ref name="Bhardwaj 2007" />

== Other research ==
Cravens has contributed significantly to other areas of space physics, including:<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/>

* Planetary [[Ionosphere]]s and [[Magnetospheres]]: His work includes modeling the ionospheres and magnetospheres of Earth, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, studying processes like ionization, chemistry, energy transport, and [[aurora]]l phenomena.<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/>
* [[Mars]]: He has developed models of the Martian upper atmosphere and ionosphere relevant to understanding atmospheric escape (including water loss) and the evolution of the Martian climate. He was a co-investigator on NASA's [[MAVEN]] (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN) mission.<ref name="MAVEN KU">{{cite web |url= https://news.ku.edu/2013/08/05/ku-professor-plays-vital-role-maven-mission-mars |title= KU professor plays vital role in MAVEN mission to Mars |publisher= KU News |date=August 5, 2013 |access-date=2025-04-10}}</ref><ref name="MAVEN NASA">{{cite web |url= https://mars.nasa.gov/maven/mission/team/ |title= MAVEN Team Directory |date= 4 December 2017 |publisher= NASA |access-date=2025-04-10}}</ref>* Outer Planets: He has studied auroral processes and atmospheric interactions at Jupiter and Saturn.<ref name="KU Physics Bio"/><ref name="Bhardwaj 2007"/>
* [[Saturn]]: Cravens was co-investigator on the Cassini Ion and Neutral Mass Spectrometer (INMS)<ref name="Cassini INMS">{{cite web |url= https://science.nasa.gov/mission/cassini/team/ |title= Cassini: The Team |publisher= NASA |date=2024-11-03 |access-date=2025-04-27}}</ref> of the [[Cassini–Huygens]] mission to Saturn.  This instrument was key in postulating a much younger age for the [[rings of Saturn]] than previously thought.<ref name="jhwaite">{{cite journal |last1=Waite |first1=J. H. |last2=Perryman |first2=R. S. |last3=Perry |first3=M. E. |last4=Miller |first4=K. E. |last5=Bell |first5=J. |last6=Cravens |first6=T. E. |last7=Glein |first7=C.
